title: Shock-wave transmission
lead: Capturing how underwater shocks transmit through PLA, aluminium and copper.
overview: My MSc thesis investigated how material and thickness influence shock transmission at solid–water interfaces. The work combined pulsed-power experiments, high-speed optical diagnostics and pressure measurements with a dedicated data-analysis workflow.
work: Conducted experiments using electrically exploding copper foils in water, with PLA, aluminium and copper samples.
Tracked transmitted and reflected fronts from high-speed shadowgraph images and analysed hydrophone measurements.
Developed the processing workflow for ROI alignment, camera-tilt correction, stack-offset correction and local shock-velocity estimation.
Compared acoustic, dynamic and nonlinear Hugoniot approaches to interface transmission.
results: The measured waves weakened with increasing sample thickness. Copper produced strongly attenuated transmitted waves, while aluminium exhibited a clear dependence on thickness. The comparison also showed why simple acoustic approximations become insufficient for stronger shocks.
limits: The conclusions apply to the tested materials, thicknesses and experimental configuration. Source coupling, material porosity and uncertainty in shock-front tracking affect the interpretation; the study is not a qualification test of a finished protective structure.

title: Sloshing control & baffle design
lead: Using transient multiphase CFD to compare passive baffles for a water-rocket tank.
overview: Project Buzz Lightyear combined a deployable-wing water rocket with a partially filled sloshing tank. My work focused on the fluid dynamics of the tank and the comparison of annular and mixed baffle configurations.
work: Led the baffled-tank CFD analysis for the two candidate designs, as documented in the team deliverable matrix.
Compared free-surface motion, lateral reaction force, centre-of-gravity displacement and oscillation frequency against the unbaffled baseline.
Contributed blockage-compliance calculations and risk assessment to the final design report.
results: The report predicts a reduction in peak lateral force from 15.4 N to 4.2 N for the mixed baffle, a 72.7% decrease relative to the unbaffled simulation. The baseline CFD frequency of 3.15 Hz was close to the analytical estimate of 3.11 Hz.
limits: These are simulation results for the report’s excitation and fill conditions. At the final-design-report stage, five requirements still awaited physical testing. Flight predictions and team hardware results should be distinguished from the sloshing CFD.

title: Thermal-vacuum coating tests
lead: Characterising spacecraft surface coatings inside KTH’s Space Sauna vacuum chamber.
overview: This group experiment examined the thermal response of four coated aluminium samples: gold plating, black anodisation, SurTec 650 and Astral ATU2230. Heater inputs and measured temperatures were used to investigate radiative exchange and transient behaviour.
work: Participated in laboratory work, report preparation and peer review, as recorded in the contribution table.
The team prepared and suspended instrumented samples inside the thermal-vacuum chamber, then adjusted heater power and recorded temperature histories.
The analysis estimated emissivity and effective heat capacity, accounting for parasitic conduction and departures from ideal equilibrium.
results: The measurements distinguished high-emissivity anodised and Astral surfaces from low-emissivity gold and SurTec surfaces. Estimated conductive losses were around 6% of the heat budget, making them a meaningful correction to the radiation-dominated balance.
limits: The LED illumination was unstable, so absorptivity could not be determined reliably. Heat-capacity estimates were sensitive to temperature slopes, measurement noise and the isothermal-sample assumption.

title: Liquid-metal heat transfer
lead: Investigating low-Prandtl-number heat transfer in two components of the TALL facility.
overview: The project modelled lead–bismuth eutectic in a single-rod heater and a counter-current straight-tube heat exchanger. The central question was how turbulence and thermal-diffusion assumptions influence the agreement between CFD and experimental temperature profiles.
work: Co-authored the group study with Antonio Morrone and Giulio Riva.
The report documents 2D axisymmetric steady-state models, temperature-dependent material properties implemented through Fluent UDFs, and mesh-sensitivity studies.
The analysis compares k–ε and k–ω SST models alongside constant and local turbulent-Prandtl-number treatments.
The heat-exchanger study includes coupled fluid–solid–fluid heat transfer and an analytical ε–NTU heat balance.
results: The report finds that a local Kays turbulent-Prandtl-number treatment improved temperature-profile agreement relative to the globally imposed alternative. Remaining discrepancies underline the importance of heat-loss assumptions and the limits of standard RANS closures for liquid metals.
limits: The supplied PDF contains figure placeholders rather than the plotted results. This page therefore summarises the written methodology and conclusions without presenting reconstructed CFD fields. The report does not assign individual ownership of its numerical tasks.

title: Satellite thermal control
lead: Sizing radiators and tuning heater duty cycles across hot, cold and survival cases.
overview: A cube-shaped satellite model was used to study thermal control under beginning- and end-of-life optical properties and seasonal orbital extremes. Analytical radiator and heater sizing was followed by numerical evaluation in SYSTEMA/THERMICA.
work: Contributed to the laboratory work, Part 2 of the report, the Lab D presentation and peer review, as documented in the contribution table.
The numerical work compared equipment temperatures with and without internal radiative exchange.
Heater powers were adjusted iteratively to reach target duty cycles in nominal cold and survival modes.
results: The final nominal cold-case duty cycles were 61.9%, 67.5% and 68.5% for the three active heaters. Internal radiation reduced the peak temperature of the hottest node by approximately 9 °C. Survival-mode tuning brought the active heaters to 61%, 67% and 62%.
limits: The model assumes a simplified geometry and prescribed thermal couplings. Some cold-case nodes reached the −10 °C lower limit, leaving tight temperature margins. These are numerical design results, separate from the MIST satellite project.

title: Two-seat electric aircraft
lead: From sizing constraints to aerodynamic performance and longitudinal stability.
overview: The team developed a conceptual two-seat general-aviation electric aircraft, using the Pipistrel Velis Electro as a starting reference. The study connected weight estimates, wing and tail geometry, aerodynamic analysis, performance and trim.
work: Co-authored the ten-person Fundamentals of Flight design report.
The team used constraint diagrams and mass estimates to establish the preliminary configuration.
The documented workflow includes airfoil selection, aerodynamic and drag analysis, mission performance, load factors and longitudinal stability.
A complete aircraft configuration was analysed with VSPAero.
results: The report’s conceptual design uses a 600 kg maximum take-off mass, a 12,000 ft cruise altitude and an 85 KCAS cruise condition. The estimated 90-minute endurance and calculated trim behaviour support the coursework concept under its stated assumptions.
limits: These are conceptual calculations, not measured flight performance or certification evidence. The report itself notes that the VSPAero results should not be used to determine post-stall behaviour. Individual task ownership is not specified.

title: Electric propulsion to the Moon
lead: Comparing propellants, thrusters and power-system mass for a lunar transfer.
overview: The study sized an electric-propulsion system for a 400 kg spacecraft travelling from geostationary transfer orbit to a lunar polar orbit. Propellant choice, thruster capability, tank mass and power generation were considered together.
work: Co-authored the mission study with Felice Venuti, Aidan Tanner and Alens Snepsts.
The team compared xenon, krypton, hydrogen and argon, using system-specific impulse as a selection criterion.
Candidate thrusters were checked against power and specific-impulse limits, with the power-generation mass included in the feasibility assessment.
results: Within the report’s assumptions, xenon and the NSTAR thruster gave the preferred configuration. The selected case reports approximately 43.24 kg of propellant and 73.6 mN average thrust for the specified transfer.
limits: This is a preliminary sizing and selection exercise. It does not establish a fully optimised low-thrust trajectory or flight-qualified propulsion system; the reported comparison depends on the assumed mission and component data.

title: Power & thermal design for Mars
lead: Integrating power, heat rejection and deployable hardware into a crewed Mars concept.
overview: The Blue Team’s Vehicle Design subgroup studied the adaptation of a Starship-based vehicle concept for a six-person Mars mission. The work integrated habitat arrangements with power, thermal control, communications, mass budgets and off-nominal scenarios.
work: Shared responsibility for power and thermal work with Koohyar Saebi, as recorded in the report appendix.
Contributed calculations and CAD for solar panels and radiators.
Worked within a multidisciplinary vehicle design that balanced subsystem needs with the overall mass and accommodation constraints.
results: The team produced a vehicle concept with subsystem layouts, requirements, budgets and contingency considerations. My contribution connected power generation and thermal management to their physical integration in the vehicle.
limits: This is an academic conceptual design, not a SpaceX project or a validated human-rated vehicle. Overall vehicle modelling and rendering are credited to other team members. Mission dates in the report are scenario assumptions.

title: Radioisotope power & radiation safety
lead: Exploring deep-space power generation, reliability and radiation protection.
overview: My bachelor’s thesis reviewed radioisotope thermoelectric generators for space missions and the radiation environment that spacecraft and crews must withstand. It connected thermoelectric conversion with mission-level power and protection considerations.
work: Reviewed RTG operating principles, fuel options and the Seebeck effect.
Compared radioisotope power with solar generation for different mission environments.
Developed an illustrative Weibull reliability analysis in MATLAB.
Examined radiation dosimetry, shielding materials and engineering and operational countermeasures.
results: The thesis presents the advantages and limitations of radioisotope power for long-duration missions and illustrates how assumed lifetime parameters influence reliability estimates.
limits: The reliability curves use assumed Weibull parameters and are an educational model, not a validated prediction of MMRTG flight reliability. The work is a literature-based thesis with analytical illustration, not reactor or RTG hardware development.

title: Active removal of space debris
role: Debris, spacecraft and cost analysis contributor
lead: An early feasibility study of foam-assisted deorbiting in low Earth orbit.
overview: This five-author group paper evaluates a spacecraft that would apply expanding foam to selected debris objects, increasing their area-to-mass ratio so atmospheric drag accelerates orbital decay. Target choice, rendezvous, propulsion and mission cost were explored at conceptual level.
work: The report credits me with paper writing and debris, spacecraft and cost analysis.
The team examined a list of ten target objects and estimated the orbit-transfer needs for visiting them.
The spacecraft concept includes Hall-effect electric propulsion and an expanding-foam delivery system.
results: The study proposes a 2,500 kg servicing spacecraft with four PPS-5000 thrusters, aiming to treat ten objects within a one-year mission. The intended subsequent deorbiting timeframe is 25 years in the study scenario.
limits: This is a preliminary feasibility study with simplified, cooperative debris and idealised foam behaviour. No rendezvous, capture or foam deployment was built or flight tested. Launch and environmental statements in the 2024 course report reflect its scenario assumptions.

title: ÆSIR hybrid rocket
lead: Hands-on propulsion work, sensor calibration and static-fire testing for Mjolnir.
overview: Mjolnir is ÆSIR’s hybrid rocket project at KTH, using paraffin fuel and nitrous oxide. Development combines propulsion modelling, mechanical integration, instrumentation and ground testing. My role in the propulsion and structures team connected analytical work with the practical preparation and assessment of static-fire tests.
work: Contributed to propulsion development, thermodynamic analysis and CFD work.
Participated in sensor calibration and static-fire testing.
Analysed load-cell measurements for thrust and oxidiser-tank loading.
results: The team’s August 2026 review brought together results from the summer static-fire campaign. Measured thrust histories were compared with propulsion predictions and used to refine the models. The review also identified fuel-regression and thermal-protection considerations for further development.
limits: The photographs and thrust comparison show team hardware and team-level test results. My contribution is described above; the campaign and its outcomes involved several team members.

title: MIST satellite
lead: Thermal modelling and subsystem requirements within a student satellite team.
overview: MIST, the MIniature Student Satellite, is a multidisciplinary spacecraft project at KTH. My work focused on thermal simulations and thermal-control requirements: understanding how heat moves through the satellite and how its components respond to the space environment.
work: Performed thermal simulations using SYSTEMA and THERMICA.
Collaborated with the team on thermal-control subsystem requirements.
results: The model views and temperature maps illustrate the relationship between spacecraft geometry, internal components and heat-transfer paths. They provide a way to examine temperature distributions and support discussions about thermal-control choices within the wider satellite team.
limits: The images are project simulation material, rather than measured in-orbit temperatures. This overview describes my thermal-analysis role and the broader team workflow; the model and mission were developed collaboratively.
